blocks.text: It is proved that שפן saphan is not the rabbit, as is claimed, but a kind of larger mouse in Eretz Yisrael, Egypt and Libya, which Herodotus and others call Δίπους [Dipous], the Elders Χοιρογρύλλιος [Choirogryllios], Jerome Ἀρκτομῦς [Arktomys], and the Arabs اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, concerning which much not yet published is brought forward from the writings of the Arabs.

In Levit, XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7., among the animals that do chew the cud but [col. 1002] do not have a cloven hoof, and are therefore unclean, השפן, ὁ σαφάν [ho saphan], is listed together with the camel and the hare. The plural שפנים sephanim occurs in Psal. CIV. 18.: The rock is a refuge לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ [tois sephanim]. And in Prov. XXX, 26.: שפנים sephanim are a feeble folk, they make their house in the rock. Most of the more recent interpreters explain them as rabbits. Many things seemingly favour this interpretation. 1. That twice in the Law השפן is joined with הארנבת, that is, with the hare, as a kindred animal. 2. That the passage of the Psalm just cited is rendered thus in the Greek edition: Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς [Petra kataphygē tois lagōois], The rock is a refuge for the hares. Some copies have τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogrylliois], that is, as they claim, for the hedgehogs. But the most ancient writers follow the former reading. Jerome, Letter 135 to Sunia and Fretela: All have rendered χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious] with a similar word; the LXX alone have translated hares. So also read Theodoret in his Commentary on this Psalm, Basil on Isaiah, chapter 2, and Apollinaris in his Paraphrase:
Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ, [Petrois ēlibatois peritharseēs eisi lagōoi,]

The hares trust in the sheer rocks; and the Arabic version, which was made from the Greek: The rock is a refuge الارانب [al-arānib] of the hares. Others combine both: thus Augustine on this passage: The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares. Arnobius: There is the rock, affording refuge either to the young of the hedgehogs, etc., or to the hares. Bede on Proverbs, chapter 30: And it should be noted that in the Psalm, where we sing „The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs, in some codices for the hares is found, in some for the choerogryllii“. 3. The Hebrew of Prov. XXX, 26., שפנים עם לא עצום, the Vulgate translator rendered thus: The little hare, a feeble folk, following, if I am not mistaken, [II, 410] some Greek translator who had explained שפנים as λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, that is, rabbits. For thus in Strabo, book 3, λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, are taken for rabbits. The Greeks have no other name for the rabbit. For κόνιλος [konilos] in Aelian, κούνικλος [kouniklos] in Polybius and Galen, words of the Spaniards, and λεβηρὶς [lebēris] in Strabo and Erotian, a word of the Massilians, were local terms not used in Greece. 4. The old Book of Names, which they ascribe to Philo, has this in Jeremiah: SAPHAN, choerogryllius, hare, or hedgehog. And in Ezekiel: SAPHAN, hedgehog, or hare. 5. In Giggeius's Arabic Lexicon, p. 854, vol. 2, سفن [safan] saphan is rendered rabbit. Where he got this from, however, I do not know at all, for I have found it nowhere else. 6. The Hebrew name שפן saphan seems to allude to the Hebrew verbs ספן and צפן, of which the former means to cover, the latter to hide. And it seems to fit the rabbit, which seeks hiding places in burrows, to lurk in them and be, as it were, covered. Martial:
The rabbit delights to dwell in dug-out caves.
